passage: In the billing department's Thursday meeting, Vikas was still opening the spreadsheet when the supervisor asked for the totals. Sunaina caught herself rolling her eyes and letting out a small sigh at the ceiling. Vikas saw it; his ears reddened and he closed the file. Afterwards, at the water cooler, Sunaina noticed how tight her own shoulders were: three deadlines, no lunch, a headache building. It was the day, not really him. She walked over to his desk. "Shall we go through the new template together? I can spare twenty minutes at four. And let's agree that totals go out by Wednesday noon, so the meeting is not a scramble." Vikas nodded, and relief loosened his face.

qa.q: What did Vikas do when Sunaina rolled her eyes?
qa.a: His ears reddened and he closed the file.

qa.q: What does Sunaina realise at the water cooler?
qa.a: That her contempt came from stress and tight shoulders, not from anything about Vikas's worth.

qa.q: What did Sunaina offer instead of mocking?
qa.a: Twenty minutes to go through the new template and a clear rule that totals go out by Wednesday noon.

qa.q: How might Vikas have felt when he saw the eye-roll?
qa.a: Embarrassed, as his reddened ears suggest, and perhaps ashamed in front of the team.

grounding: The protagonist looks down on a slower colleague, sees the contempt reflects stress and pride, and offers help and clear expectations instead of mocking.

passage: Confidential note from Madhuri, member of the workplace committee. Vandana came to see me on Tuesday, unsure whether what she had experienced was "serious enough." She said a senior colleague had been commenting on her appearance, and once put a hand on her shoulder after she had told him to stop. She had not reported it because she doubted herself. I told her it is serious, that it is not her fault, and that she did not need a name for it to be allowed to speak. Together we wrote down the dates and what was said. She then told the colleague, in writing, that the comments must stop. I explained the committee's steps, and she chose to file a formal complaint that same day. I checked in with her on Thursday and again a week later.

qa.q: What did Vandana tell the colleague in writing?
qa.a: She told him that the comments must stop.

qa.q: Why had Vandana not reported it earlier?
qa.a: She doubted herself and wondered whether it was serious enough.

qa.q: What did Madhuri do after listening to Vandana?
qa.a: Madhuri said it was serious and not her fault, wrote down the dates and words with her, explained the committee's steps and checked in later.

qa.q: How might Vandana have felt on hearing that it was serious?
qa.a: She may have felt relieved to be believed, though possibly still nervous about filing.

grounding: A committee member's note shows a colleague's unwanted remarks and touch being taken seriously, with a clear no, written details and use of the committee.

passage:
Subject: Thank you, properly

Dear Mridul,

When my father was taken to hospital on Monday night, I sent you three lines and vanished for four days. You took the vendor call, redid my slides for the Thursday review, and told our manager I was "handling something" without asking a single question. I do not think I said how much that meant. I am back now, and I would like to take the Friday client visit off you, since you mentioned dreading the drive. Lunch is on me as well. And if you are ever in a crunch, tell me before it gets bad.

Gratefully,
Eshaan

qa.q: What did Mridul do for the Thursday review?
qa.a: Mridul redid Eshaan's slides.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan write instead of just thanking in passing?
qa.a: Eshaan felt indebted and thought the thanks had not been said properly.

qa.q: How does Eshaan plan to return the favour?
qa.a: By taking over the Friday client visit, paying for lunch and offering help before a crunch gets bad.

qa.q: How might Mridul have felt about covering without questions?
qa.a: Mridul was probably willing to help, and not asking any questions shows trust.

grounding: A colleague who was covered for during a family emergency thanks the colleague sincerely and offers to return the favour at the right time.

passage: Gurleen, you are fuming about the drilling upstairs, so listen. When I was twenty-five I lived beneath a man who rehearsed tabla at night. For three weeks I lay awake composing speeches. One night I stood in the stairwell, fists clenched, and thought: if I knock now, I will say something ugly. I went back inside. The next Sunday I knocked with a plate of pakoras and said, "I love the music, but after ten I hear every beat through the ceiling. Could you play before nine, or put a mat under the drum?" He blinked, then laughed, and slid a folded blanket under it that same evening. If he had not, I had the society rules to fall back on. I never needed them. Talk first, Gurleen. Kishore

qa.q: What did Kishore bring when knocking on the neighbour's door?
qa.a: Kishore brought a plate of pakoras.

qa.q: Why did Kishore go back inside from the stairwell?
qa.a: Kishore's anger was high and Kishore feared saying something ugly.

qa.q: What specific fix did Kishore propose?
qa.a: To play before nine or put a mat under the drum.

qa.q: How did the neighbour respond to the request?
qa.a: He blinked, then laughed, and put a folded blanket under the drum that same evening.

grounding: An elder recalls building irritation at a neighbour's noise, speaking calmly before it exploded and proposing a specific fix.

passage:
Monday. Sarita from the flat below stood in the corridor and shouted that Vijay's plant pots were dripping onto her laundry. A few doors opened a crack. Vijay's temper rose and the reply was hot on the tongue, but Vijay took a breath and said, "I can hear that this has upset you. Can we look at it tomorrow evening, just the two of us?"

Tuesday. They met at the balcony. Vijay saw a cracked saucer under one pot and offered to bring the pots inside and put trays under the rest. Sarita's voice dropped. "Fine. And I should not have shouted like that."

A week later. There were no more complaints. Sarita left a bag of curry leaves at Vijay's door.

qa.q: What was dripping onto Sarita's laundry?
qa.a: Water from Vijay's plant pots was dripping onto it.

qa.q: How can you tell that Vijay was angry but kept it in check?
qa.a: Vijay's temper rose and the reply was hot on the tongue, yet Vijay took a breath and offered to talk the next evening.

qa.q: What fix did Vijay offer for the dripping?
qa.a: To bring the pots inside and put trays under the rest.

qa.q: How did Sarita seem to feel by the end?
qa.a: Calmer and a little sorry, since she apologised for shouting and later left curry leaves.

grounding: A neighbour shouts over a small matter; the protagonist stays calm, offers to settle it privately later and avoids an audience.

passage: At the housing society's front office, the guard slid a slip across the desk: Joseph's parcel had been signed for by Reena in 4B, again. Joseph took the stairs with a box of ladoos. Three weeks earlier, when Joseph's father slipped in the bathroom during a night shift, it was Reena who heard the thud, sat with him, and waited until Joseph got home. Joseph rang the bell. "Nothing to thank for," Reena said, but took the box. Joseph added, "My number is on the society list, and I am only two floors up, any hour." Reena smiled and kept the door half open, as always, and Joseph did not step inside.

qa.q: Who signed for Joseph's parcel?
qa.a: Reena in 4B signed for it.

qa.q: Why did Joseph bring a box of ladoos?
qa.a: Joseph felt grateful for the help with parcels and for the night Joseph's father slipped.

qa.q: How can Joseph respect Reena's privacy while returning the kindness?
qa.a: By offering help and a number, and not stepping inside when Reena keeps the door half open.

qa.q: How might Reena see the visit?
qa.a: Reena said there was nothing to thank for and took the box, which suggests modesty and ease with quiet help.

grounding: A neighbour who helps with parcels and an ageing parent is thanked warmly while their privacy is respected.

passage: Ines was carrying groceries up the stairs of her building in Porto when Bao, from the second floor, leaned out of his doorway. "Another visitor on Saturday," he said. "And you work such odd hours." Two women on the landing stopped talking as she passed. Ines felt watched and a little small. She could have snapped. Instead she said, "Good morning, Mr Bao. Yes, my sister visits on weekends, and I work in the hospital lab. Have a nice day." She kept the smile plain and walked on, jaw slightly tight. Upstairs she put the kettle on and told herself: they can wonder, but they do not decide how I live. On Sunday she still left Bao a polite note about the broken lift light.

qa.q: Where does Ines work?
qa.a: Ines works in the hospital lab.

qa.q: How can you tell that Ines felt watched?
qa.a: The two women stopped talking as she passed, and she felt a little small with a slightly tight jaw.

qa.q: How could Ines stay courteous while keeping her boundaries?
qa.a: By answering plainly and briefly without over-explaining and without hostility, as she did.

qa.q: How might Bao see his own questions?
qa.a: Bao may see them as friendly interest, though to Ines they feel like scrutiny.

grounding: Neighbours are curious and judgmental about visitors and work; the protagonist stays courteous, keeps boundaries and does not let gossip decide her life.

passage: In the clinic's waiting room, Minakshi, feverish, was asked for an emergency contact on the form. She stared at the blank line. She knew no one in the building by name, only by flat number. The woman beside her said, "Aren't you from 5C? I'm Bhavna, 5B." Minakshi had passed her for a year with only a nod. Bhavna wrote her number on the back of a prescription slip and said, "For emergencies. Not for chats." Minakshi almost smiled. That evening she stuck the number on her fridge, knocked on 5B. "I like my quiet," she said, "but let's swap numbers properly."

qa.q: Which flat does Bhavna live in?
qa.a: Bhavna lives in 5B.

qa.q: Why did the blank emergency contact line matter to Minakshi?
qa.a: It made her realise she had nobody nearby to call, since she had kept to herself and knew neighbours only by flat number.

qa.q: What small step built safety and belonging for Minakshi?
qa.a: Swapping numbers properly and greeting the neighbour, while still keeping her privacy.

qa.q: What might it be like for Bhavna to offer her number?
qa.a: Bhavna is friendly but respects privacy, as "for emergencies, not for chats" shows.

grounding: The protagonist prefers privacy, but a moment in a clinic shows that small contact with a neighbour builds safety and belonging.

passage: Joseph carried folding chairs down to the courtyard of the Chennai housing society, where the meeting about the joint festival programme was about to begin. Reena, the treasurer, was counting steel plates. Two years ago Joseph had known only the lift button; last month, hearing the speakers crackle at the Pongal gathering, Joseph had offered to fix them. Tonight a resident asked, "Why must every festival be squeezed into one programme?" Joseph said, "Last year our Christmas star hung beside Mrs Iyer's kolam and nobody minded. I'd like to sing, and I'll bring the speakers." Reena wrote "sound: Joseph" on the sheet and looked up. "Come Saturday for the rangoli too." Joseph walked back up feeling that the whole building was, a little, home.

qa.q: What did Joseph offer to bring to the festival?
qa.a: Joseph offered to bring the speakers.

qa.q: How does Joseph feel about being part of the society now?
qa.a: Joseph feels included, walking back up with the sense that the whole building is a little bit home, after knowing only the lift button two years ago.

qa.q: How does Joseph show that belonging is built by showing up?
qa.a: By carrying chairs, fixing the speakers and offering time and skill for the shared festival.

qa.q: Why might the resident who asked about squeezing every festival into one programme have been unsure?
qa.a: The resident may have worried about crowding, and Joseph's example of the star beside Mrs Iyer's kolam shows differences sitting side by side.

grounding: The protagonist joins festivals and residents' meetings, contributes time and skills and respects differences, feeling at home through showing up.

subtopic: Being idolised or hated by juniors
passage: Manjula, you say your junior writes down every word you say as if it were scripture. I had a junior like that when I was twenty-six, a young man named Ravi. I loved it, honestly. I also felt uneasy, because I knew my advice on client calls was mostly luck. One day he rewrote a whole quotation because I had "sounded sure," and it cost us the deal. I told him plainly that I had been guessing, and that I had made three mistakes myself that month. After that I began asking him, "What would you do? Why?" before I answered. He hated it at first. Later he started disagreeing with me, and I saw that admiration can either bind a person to you or help them stand up. Be careful which one you feed. Devika

qa.q: What did Ravi change because Devika sounded sure?
qa.a: He rewrote a whole quotation, and it cost the deal.

qa.q: Why did Devika feel uneasy about Ravi's admiration?
qa.a: Devika knew that the advice on client calls was mostly luck and did not deserve to be treated as gospel.

qa.q: What did Devika start doing to encourage independent thinking?
qa.a: Asking Ravi what he would do and why before giving an answer.

qa.q: How did Ravi react at first to being asked?
qa.a: He hated it at first but later began disagreeing, which shows growing independence.

grounding: An elder recalls a junior who treated every word as gospel, and how sharing mistakes and asking the junior to think built independence.
